newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-DASA doing better after horror year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-DASA doing better after horror year.

text.p: Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) said on Thursday it expected sales to grow by around six percent this year after turning in a "substantially better" performance last year.

Chief executive Manfred Bischoff told reporters group sales climbed 13 percent in 1996 to 13 billion marks ($7.7 billion), while incoming orders -- boosted by new Airbus business -- surged 54 percent to 16.9 billion marks.
"We will be substantially better than in 1995 and substantially above what we had planned," said Bischoff.
But he would not give detailed 1996 profit figures ahead of the announcement of Daimler-Benz AG group results in April.
Speaking at the aerospace group's annual news conference in Munich, he said all but one of DASA's divisions -- defence and civil systems -- made a profit last year.
The aircraft, defence and space company plunged to a net loss of four billion marks in 1995, pushing parent Daimler-Benz AG to the biggest group net loss in German corporate history.

The preliminary figures published were based for the first time on the U.S. GAAP accounting standards and stripped out results from companies disposed of in 1995 and 1996 -- which included plane makers Fokker and Dornier Luftfahrt.

As originally reported group turnover was 15 billion marks in 1995, but Bischoff said that on a comparable 1995 sales were adjusted to 11.5 billion marks to reflect divestments. DASA has forecast an operating loss of 780 million marks in 1996.
Turnover gains came in the aero-engine and space sector, where turnover was up 35 percent and 10.5 percent respectively.

Aircraft turnover, based on DASA's Airbus production, rose 13 percent to six billion marks. Airbus orders trebled last year to 326 aircraft -- worth 23.6 billion marks. That figure does not, however, include a huge order from USAir, which has not yet been finalised, Bischoff said.

Looking ahead, the number of deliveries of the Airbus A319, A320 and A321 models will rise from 130 this year to 207 in 1999, he added. Airbus links DASA, British Aerospace, France's Aerospatiale and CASA of Spain.
Strong aircraft orders have led management to scale back job cuts and launch a 280 million mark investment programme -- most going to DASA's Airbus fuselage plant in Hamburg.

DASA still plans to reduce its workforce to 42,500 this year from 44,900 at end-1996 under a cost-cutting scheme intended to make the company viable even if the dollar-mark exchange rate returns to its 1995 low of 1.35.
Recent dollar gains -- in which aircraft and defence products are priced -- will not be fully reflected in results due to DASA's currency hedging stratgegy, Bischoff said.
Only DASA's civil and defence systems group suffered a fall in sales last year of one percent to 2.6 billion marks, and is expected to post a loss.

Bischoff called for "stability" in defence planning to help European aerospace companies compete against U.S. competitors -- led by newly-merged Boeing-McDonnell Douglas -- which enjoy the full backing of the Washington government.

Pivotal to the future of DASA's defence operations is an order by the German government of the four-country Eurofighter 2000 combat aircraft. DASA's partners are British Aerospace, Alenia ALEI.RO of Italy and CASA.

Despite delays to a decision by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on placing a firm order for the 180 Eurofighters, Bischoff said he was optimistic of a positive result and winning the backing of the German parliament.
"I am optimistic that, despite massive cuts in the defence budget, the order for the Eurofighter will come," he said.
Bischoff added that DASA had phased out its divisional structure and brought in top managers in operating areas to create a broad decision-making structure with a five-man board.
Without specifying in which areas, he added that acquisitions as well as disposals were likely this year.
($ = 1.684 German Marks)
